Water Crisis in Cape Town

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Cape Town has a water crisis at present and restrictions may soon go up to level 4 which means no watering allowed at all. We are not saving enough water in the Cape. The target is 800 million litres per week. We are on 975 million at present and our dams are now at 40% and a weak winter rainfall is expected. The real drama lies for next summer. We will ride along with Enforcement agencies as they go and penalise people who disobey water restrictions. We will also show how water activists are trying to outdo each other on Social Media in their attempts to save water and we will also give examples of how cheap it is to set a greywater system. What is doing the rounds at the moment is that people are saying what about all the mountain springs and the canal system in Cape Town City. We will briefly explore that.

We will also touch upon fascinating long term solutions which include this unique deep aquifer system in the Western Cape which holds billions of litres of fresh drinking water and the city work with the geological agency to efficiently find way to access it. A micro example of how the city should operate is 1 case study - Hermanus where a borehole system taps into the upper reaches of the deep aquifer and supplies a third of the town's water. We will also look at planes to purify water from the lower lying Cape Flats Aquifer.


I think the overall message is that cities and individuals are being forced into changing their perception that water is to be respected in terms of our ever increasing droughts and erratic weather patterns.

Monwabisi Gwijila

Press Release:


Cape Water Crisis
The Western Cape has been hit by a crippling drought and dam levels have dropped to below 40 percent, of which less than 30 percent is usable. Unless heavy rains fall soon, the city could face a massive water crisis which can only be averted if citizens adhere to strict, never-before implemented, level 3B water restrictions. But how is it possible that, a mere 90-minute drive from Cape Town in the coastal town of Hermanus, no water restrictions are needed? Carte Blanche asks: could the solution lurk deep underground?


Script:


The western cape region is in the midst of a crippling drought, as a result of 2 years of below average rainfall. This is because of changing weather patterns and the effects of global warming.

Kevin Winter: This is the third warmest year in succession. 2016 broke all the records one again.


Rising temperatures and increased wind speeds over storage water is increasing the evaporation. Six main dams supply the city and surrounding agricultural areas. They are at 39.2% capacity but of that only 29 percent is usable as the last ten per cent is difficult to extract. Never before has the city had to implement level 3B restrictions which drastically limit the use of potable water for gardening and irrigation. Dr. Kevin Winter says that the cape will be in real trouble if the low levels of rainfall continue as predicted.

Kevin Winter: What we have got to be looking to is what do our dams look like by the time we come to the end of August, if they are less than 80% full, we are going to really struggle when it comes to April, May the next year and that is our worry if we even get to that point.

The short term solution lies with consumers who the city is trying to limit to 800 million liters per day. Xanthea Limberg is in the hot seat.

Xanthea Limber: This new week, we've seen a slight drop sitting at 807 million of water usage per day. So we are still 7 million above our desired target.

The city is hoping it wont have to introduce water rationing as a last resort.

Xanthea Limberg: The city of cape towns water services department has been working tirelessly behind the scenes on a range of initiatives both medium and long term plans that look at tapping into alternative sources of water.

Retired associate professor and internationally renowned scientist Chris Hartnady has been doing just that. He is the technical director of a consulting firm that has has been working with the city for the past 16 years exploring the possibility of extracting billions of liters of water confined in a deep lying aquifer under the The Table Mountain group formation. It stretches from Vanrhynsdorp to cape town to Port Elizabeth. We travelled with him to to a drilling site near Steen bras dam to find out more about untapped resource deep below the surface.

Chris Hartnady: it is important because it is a very large aquifer. Probably of its kind, one of the largest in the world and quite unique. You don’t get thousand-meter thick quartz sites every where and anywhere.

The only other geological formation with the same rock structure is the Roraima super group in south America

LINK: This 450-million-year old rock lies at the surface of the mountains of the South Western Cape. It's incredibly hard but it does crack and fissure which means that water can seep through it.

Kilometers down in the faults of the Quartz rocks water is accumulated which form the aquifers.

Chris Hartnady: And it percolates down to these deep basins structures.

John: Through the cracks and the fissures?

Chris Hartnady: Its the cracks and the fissures and again the key thing is the strength of the rocks means that those fissures can remain open to depths of approaching 10km.

The Table Mountain group aquifer Project was initiated by the city of cape town, in 2001 Hartnady and his team began working on this multi phase operation. After extensive geological and environmental impact studies digging began in 3 designate sites in 2005.

John: It is clearly a very long process, its not something that happens overnight?

Prof. Hartnady: It doesn’t happen overnight and of course drilling into rocks which are almost pure quartz, on Mohs Hardness scale, its up at 7 just below topaz and diamonds.

John: So does that mean very hard?

Chris Hartnady: That means very hard and very strong... this is tough stuff.

They went down 700 meters in Outdshorn and struck the upper reaches of the aquifer This bore hole had an initial yield of 60 litres per second. Several more boreholes are in the pipeline.

John: Good quality water?
Chris hartnady: Good quality water. A little bit iron rich and manganese rich because it reacts with the rocks cement

And this water form the Table Mountain Group Aquifer is being put to good use in one town in particular to alleviate the effects of the drought.

LINK: Hermanus is just an hour and half’s drive from cape town and yet unlike the mother city's residents, the people here aren’t constantly talking about a water crisis and that’s because, well, there isn’t one.

A single dam supplies hermanus but drought and increasing population meant that the town was running out of water and something urgently had to be done. Hartnady and his team worked with the Overstrand municipality and struck water 200 meters down. Several boreholes were dug and they became operational in 2011. The boreholes in and around hermanus have been licensed to draw 3.2 Billion litres of water per year. Steven Muller is director of infrastructure and planning for the area.

Steven Muller: Its a more secure source for us, here it is about 200m underground so its not polluted, it doesnt evaporate, its just sitting there waiting for us to take it.

As a result, the dam is 80% capacity as the aquifer supplies up to 30% of the towns need. But the amount of water taken from the aquifer has to be strictly monitored.

Muller: We don’t want to deplete the aquifer so that sea water intrudes into the aquifer so we manage it on water levels, on the salinity of the water that comes out so there is a lot of different parameters that we measure on a continuous basis.


The water does contain Iron and Manganese but a unique biological method, the first of its type in south Africa, is being used to clean it.

Muller: We use bacteria that live on iron and manganese so with the right ph. and the right amount of oxygen, you have bacteria that clean the water, so its a very environmentally friendly process and quite a cheap process.

Despite the success at hermanus, the city of cape town put the pilot phase of the Table Mountain group aquifer project on hold in 2011. Its now due to come back on track in 2024.

John: So it may have taken this particular crisis to reinvigorate the city of cape town around this particular project?

Hartnady: well we hope so and energy is what is needed because obviously in a project like this where you are challenged both geologically and technically - as I say the drilling is not an inconsiderable technical problem. But we are still there and we hope that we can move forward.

Another long term solution will come online in 2021 when new infrastructure will pump additional water from the berg river into the Voelvlei dam... The city says it is also exploring desalination but at this stage the answer to the drought lies with the residents, and that’s according to Dr Mao Amis who head up the African Centre for a Green Economy

Dr Amis: It is the softer solutions ultimately that will bring us out of this water crisis because it is the consumer led type of behavior change is required to bring about the water conservation that this city and south Africa needs.

Kieno: Its a crisis level. If one just looks at the numbers!

The media have come on board to stress the need to save water and nothing irks radio show host Kieno Kammies more than when he hears of residents fluting the restrictions, He even posted this video of a man using potable water to wash down his property.

Kieno: Some of the excuses he uses. He tells me "oh no its chlorinated, we should be using that water in any case." We cannot be having this type of wreck less behavior!

Xanthea: It both surprises me and infuriates me that that is the case because since the inception of level 1 water restrictions we have attempted to make people aware and educate them about the water supply conditions within the region.

Fortunately, there now seems to be a growing awareness with many residents heading the call and taking to social media. they are posting pictures of their water saving contraption and sharing information on how to save every drop. Supply companies are working around the clock to install grey water systems but these come at a price.

LINK: To a lay person like me, who doesn’t really understand the difference between one wrench and another, the idea of installing even a simple grey water system is, well, a little bit daunting,

So it was for Sarah Rushmere but she is fortunate to know Monwabisi Gwijila. He recently qualified as a plumber and he installed a simple gray water system on the property at a very reasonable price. Sarah posted his work on social media and jobs have started to flow in for him. In fact, the interest demanded that he set up his own Facebook page.

Monwabisi: We have done this Facebook page and quite a lot of interest came along with it and even with me it gave me that sense, it looks like this is a business to stick around.

Sarah Rushemere: I think it is a massive opportunity for plumbers who might otherwise be under employed or unemployed to do fantastic things for people at the moment and be almost like a water wise advisor.

Whilst the city encourages grey water systems, the real solutions lie in the long term.

Mao Amis: Water requires significant long term planning. So to put a water infrastructure in now, it will really take effect in 10, 20 years. So from a leadership perspective we do need to have the long term planning, understanding where our water is actually coming from.

Hartnady is confident that the water confined within the unique geological makeup of the Table Mountain Group Aquifer will save the day.

Hartnady: We don’t get these things everywhere. we’ve got this opportunity here; we should relish what we have.

Muller: We don’t want to deplete the aquifer so that sea water intrudes into the aquifer so we manage it on water levels, on the salinity of the water that comes out so there is a lot of different parameters that we measure on a continuous basis. The water does contain Iron and Manganese but a unique biological method, the first of its type in south Africa, is being used to clean it. Muller: We use bacteria that live on iron and manganese so with the right ph. and the right amount of oxygen, you have bacteria that clean the water, so its a very environmentally friendly process and quite a cheap process. Despite the success at hermanus, the city of cape town put the pilot phase of the Table Mountain group aquifer project on hold in 2011. Its now due to come back on track in 2024. John: So it may have taken this particular crisis to reinvigorate the city of cape town around this particular project? Hartnady: well we hope so and energy is what is needed because obviously in a project like this where you are challenged both geologically and technically - as I say the drilling is not an inconsiderable technical problem. But we are still there and we hope that we can move forward. Another long term solution will come online in 2021 when new infrastructure will pump additional water from the berg river into the Voelvlei dam... The city says it is also exploring desalination but at this stage the answer to the drought lies with the residents, and that’s according to Dr Mao Amis who head up the African Centre for a Green Economy Dr Amis: It is the softer solutions ultimately that will bring us out of this water crisis because it is the consumer led type of behavior change is required to bring about the water conservation that this city and south Africa needs. Kieno: Its a crisis level. If one just looks at the numbers! The media have come on board to stress the need to save water and nothing irks radio show host Kieno Kammies more than when he hears of residents fluting the restrictions, He even posted this video of a man using potable water to wash down his property. Kieno: Some of the excuses he uses. He tells me "oh no its chlorinated, we should be using that water in any case." We cannot be having this type of wreck less behavior! Xanthea: It both surprises me and infuriates me that that is the case because since the inception of level 1 water restrictions we have attempted to make people aware and educate them about the water supply conditions within the region. Fortunately, there now seems to be a growing awareness with many residents heading the call and taking to social media. they are posting pictures of their water saving contraption and sharing information on how to save every drop. Supply companies are working around the clock to install grey water systems but these come at a price. LINK: To a lay person like me, who doesn’t really understand the difference between one wrench and another, the idea of installing even a simple grey water system is, well, a little bit daunting, So it was for Sarah Rushmere but she is fortunate to know Monwabisi Gwijila. He recently qualified as a plumber and he installed a simple gray water system on the property at a very reasonable price. Sarah posted his work on social media and jobs have started to flow in for him. In fact, the interest demanded that he set up his own Facebook page. Monwabisi: We have done this Facebook page and quite a lot of interest came along with it and even with me it gave me that sense, it looks like this is a business to stick around. Sarah Rushemere: I think it is a massive opportunity for plumbers who might otherwise be under employed or unemployed to do fantastic things for people at the moment and be almost like a water wise advisor. Whilst the city encourages grey water systems, the real solutions lie in the long term. Mao Amis: Water requires significant long term planning. So to put a water infrastructure in now, it will really take effect in 10, 20 years. So from a leadership perspective we do need to have the long term planning, understanding where our water is actually coming from. Hartnady is confident that the water confined within the unique geological makeup of the Table Mountain Group Aquifer will save the day. Hartnady: We don’t get these things everywhere. we’ve got this opportunity here; we should relish what we have. . metadata.Summary: Cape Town has a water crisis at present and restrictions may soon go up to level 4 which means no watering allowed at all. We are not saving enough water in the Cape. The target is 800 million litres per week. We are on 975 million at present and our dams are now at 40% and a weak winter rainfall is expected. The real drama lies for next summer. We will ride along with Enforcement agencies as they go and penalise people who disobey water restrictions. We will also show how water activists are trying to outdo each other on Social Media in their attempts to save water and we will also give examples of how cheap it is to set a greywater system. What is doing the rounds at the moment is that people are saying what about all the mountain springs and the canal system in Cape Town City. We will briefly explore that. We will also touch upon fascinating long term solutions which include this unique deep aquifer system in the Western Cape which holds billions of litres of fresh drinking water and the city work with the geological agency to efficiently find way to access it. A micro example of how the city should operate is 1 case study - Hermanus where a borehole system taps into the upper reaches of the deep aquifer and supplies a third of the town's water. We will also look at planes to purify water from the lower lying Cape Flats Aquifer. I think the overall message is that cities and individuals are being forced into changing their perception that water is to be respected in terms of our ever increasing droughts and erratic weather patterns.
